meta.title: Tracing with OpenTelemetry and OpenLLMetry
meta.thesis: Tracing with OpenTelemetry and OpenLLMetry is practical when learners can apply it to this concrete case: An LLM workflow needs traces that connect web requests, model calls, retrievers, and tools. By the end, they should be able to build or review OpenTelemetry span plan for LLM and retrieval operations, measure percentage of incidents with end-to-end trace coverage, and catch the failure where model calls are visible but disconnected from the request that triggered them.

modules.title: Telemetry standards give model calls portable shape
modules.sub: Start with why a GenAI trace should not be trapped in one vendor.
modules.summary: OpenTelemetry provides a shared language for spans and metrics.
objectives: Explain why LLM-specific traces need standard attributes.
Separate vendor-neutral telemetry from product-specific metadata.

blocks.title: A standard span is a migration strategy

spans.text: Problem anchor: an enterprise support agent starts in Langfuse, adds Phoenix for experiments, and still needs infrastructure traces in its existing APM. If each tool names model calls, token counts, and retrieval steps differently, release analysis becomes translation work.

OpenTelemetry gives the application a common trace model: spans, attributes, metrics, context propagation, and export. The GenAI semantic conventions add LLM-specific names for operations such as chat, embeddings, retrieval, tools, agents, and token usage. The KB notes that these conventions are still development-oriented, so version pinning and local documentation matter as of 2026-06-22.

blocks.title: Case study: backend migration without losing eval history

spans.text: A team keeps span names like gen_ai.chat and app.retrieval.search stable while exporting to a new backend. Their dashboards survive because model, provider, prompt version, token counts, source IDs, and release SHA are attributes rather than hidden in vendor-specific event text.

blocks.title: Standardization reason
blocks.prompt: Why use OpenTelemetry-style GenAI attributes for LLM calls?

options.text: To avoid recording any model metadata.
To make traces queryable and portable across telemetry backends.
To replace all product evals with infrastructure metrics.

blocks.explanation: Standards help preserve meaning across tools, but they do not choose your product thresholds.

modules.title: Context propagation keeps agent steps in one story
modules.sub: Parent-child span relationships are the backbone of trace meaning.
modules.summary: Trace context connects retrieval, tool calls, and model calls into one run.
objectives: Explain trace ID, span ID, and parent span in an LLM workflow.
Spot orphan spans that break root-cause analysis.
Design context propagation through async tools and workers.

blocks.title: No parent context, no agent story

spans.text: An agent run crosses function calls, async jobs, external APIs, and maybe a human approval queue. The trace ID says these spans belong to the same user request. Parent span IDs say which operation caused which child operation.

For a support refund agent, answer_request is the parent. retrieve_policy and account_lookup are children. draft_answer depends on both. validate_policy_citation and score_groundedness are children of the draft. If account_lookup is orphaned, the trace cannot prove which user answer used that tool result.

blocks.title: Trace tree for a refund agent

spans.text: answer_request -> classify_intent -> retrieve_policy -> account_lookup -> draft_answer -> validate_citation -> score_groundedness. That order is not just decoration. It encodes causality: retrieval and account lookup supply evidence; drafting consumes it; validation and scoring judge the result.
Spaced recall: compare this to the Langfuse span tree. The tool changes; the causal trace idea stays the same.

modules.title: OpenLLMetry maps LLM frameworks into spans
modules.sub: Auto-instrumentation accelerates tracing but does not define your product contract.
modules.summary: OpenLLMetry can collect common LLM spans while you fill product-specific gaps.
objectives: Describe what auto-instrumentation is useful for.
Name fields that often need manual enrichment.
Avoid assuming generated traces prove product quality.

spans.text: OpenLLMetry is useful because it can instrument popular LLM libraries and export spans through OpenTelemetry. That reduces the toil of wrapping every model call by hand. But auto-instrumentation cannot know your refund policy source IDs, approval rule, customer tier, or eval rubric unless your app adds them.
The design rule is simple: let auto-instrumentation capture common model and framework details; add manual spans or attributes for product decisions.

objectives: Write a small contract check for GenAI span attributes.

blocks.title: Contract check for OpenTelemetry-style GenAI spans

spans.text: This is a lightweight contract test around the telemetry your app exports. It uses OpenTelemetry-style naming plus app-specific attributes for retrieval and prompt version.

predictThenReveal.prompt: Predict what happens if app.prompt_version is removed from the gen_ai.chat span.
predictThenReveal.answer: The check reports missing app.prompt_version on gen_ai.chat. The model call still has token data, but release comparison cannot group the run by prompt version.

modules.title: Export boundaries protect secrets and budgets
modules.sub: Collectors, sampling, and redaction decide what leaves the app.
modules.summary: Advanced tracing requires governance at the telemetry export boundary.
objectives: Explain why raw prompts and tool outputs need redaction.
Set sampling rules that preserve rare failures.
Avoid high-cardinality attributes that ruin dashboards.

blocks.title: The exporter is a policy boundary

spans.text: OpenTelemetry makes it easy to send traces to many backends. That flexibility increases the need for controls. Redact raw prompts when possible, store source IDs instead of full private documents, sample successful low-risk runs, preserve severe failures, and document which attributes are allowed to leave the app.

items.text: Privacy failure: exporting raw tool output with customer account details.
Cost failure: tracing every token-heavy success path without sampling.
Dashboard failure: adding user IDs or query text to span names.
Reliability failure: changing convention versions without a migration note.

blocks.ruleOfThumb: Export standardized metadata broadly; export sensitive content narrowly or not at all.
blocks.useWhen: You need cross-backend tracing, release comparison, or framework-agnostic telemetry. The team can maintain attribute conventions and redaction rules. OpenLLMetry covers common spans and manual annotations fill product gaps.
blocks.avoidWhen: The workflow contains highly sensitive data and no collector policy exists. A single product-specific observability platform already satisfies the near-term need. The team cannot version or test the exported span contract.

blocks.title: Export policy
blocks.prompt: What is the safest default for retrieved private document text in exported traces?

options.text: Put the full document text in every span name.
Store stable source IDs and redacted snippets unless raw content is explicitly allowed.
Drop all metadata, including model and prompt version.

blocks.explanation: Useful tracing preserves meaning while respecting data boundaries.

eval.label: Eval
eval.laymanDefinition: A repeatable test of model or system behavior against expected criteria.
eval.technicalNote: In these lessons, evals are release evidence: they combine cases, assertions, scores, and review rules.

trace.label: Trace
trace.laymanDefinition: A structured record of one run, including spans, inputs, outputs, metadata, and scores.
trace.technicalNote: Traces make failures diagnosable by showing which retrieval, model, tool, or scoring step produced the result.

dataset.label: Dataset
dataset.laymanDefinition: A curated set of examples used for evaluation, debugging, or regression checks.
dataset.technicalNote: A useful eval dataset stores inputs, expected behavior, metadata slices, and source or rubric references.

judge.label: LLM-as-judge
judge.laymanDefinition: An LLM used to grade or compare outputs with a rubric.
judge.technicalNote: LLM judges are semantic scorers, not final authority; their prompts, model, thresholds, and spot checks must be versioned.

regression.label: Regression
regression.laymanDefinition: A previously working behavior that breaks after a prompt, model, data, or code change.
regression.technicalNote: Regression testing protects known capabilities and safety boundaries while allowing harmless wording variation.

rubric.label: Rubric
rubric.laymanDefinition: A scoring guide that states what a good answer or run must demonstrate.
rubric.technicalNote: Rubrics make qualitative judgment reviewable by naming criteria, severity, examples, and thresholds.

finalCheck.title: Knowledge check
finalCheck.intro: A quick check across the whole lesson — pick or type your answers.

questions.prompt: An LLM agent makes three sequential tool calls, but in your trace backend each tool call appears as a top-level root span with no parent. What is the most likely cause?

options.text: The model name attribute is missing from the GenAI span.
Context propagation was not threaded through the async tool workers, so each call started a fresh trace.
The sampling rate was set too low, dropping the parent span.
OpenLLMetry auto-instrumentation does not support tool calls.

questions.explanation: When the trace context (trace ID + parent span ID) is not forwarded into async workers or tool handlers, each one opens a brand-new root span, producing orphan spans that break root-cause analysis.

questions.prompt: You are writing a contract check that runs in CI to guard your release pipeline. Which single missing GenAI span attribute would most directly break latency-by-model analysis in your dashboard?

options.text: gen_ai.system (the LLM provider name)
gen_ai.request.model (the model identifier)
gen_ai.usage.prompt_tokens (input token count)
http.status_code (the HTTP response code)

questions.explanation: Latency-by-model queries group and filter on gen_ai.request.model; without it every span is unattributable to a specific model, making the analysis impossible.

questions.prompt: Your team enables OpenLLMetry auto-instrumentation and sees spans for every OpenAI call. A colleague concludes the traces prove the prompts are high quality. What is wrong with that conclusion?

options.text: Auto-instrumentation only captures metadata like model name and token counts — it cannot measure prompt quality or output correctness.
Auto-instrumentation is unreliable and frequently drops spans.
OpenLLMetry does not support OpenAI, so the spans are fabricated.
Span data is always redacted before export, so quality cannot be assessed.

questions.explanation: Auto-instrumentation records structural telemetry (latency, token usage, model name) but has no way to evaluate whether a prompt or response is semantically correct or high quality — that requires separate evaluation logic.

questions.prompt: You want to add a span attribute that identifies which tool an agent called. Which naming choice best protects your dashboard from cardinality explosion?

options.text: tool.invocation_id — a UUID generated per call
tool.input_payload — the full JSON body sent to the tool
tool.name — a fixed label like 'web_search' or 'calculator'
tool.timestamp_ms — the Unix millisecond timestamp of the call

questions.explanation: Low-cardinality attributes like a fixed tool name group cleanly in dashboards; UUIDs, payloads, and timestamps each create a unique value per call, exploding index cardinality and making aggregation useless.

questions.prompt: Explain two distinct reasons why raw LLM prompt text should be redacted or excluded before spans are exported to a third-party observability backend.
questions.acceptableAnswer: Any two of: (1) Prompts may contain PII or sensitive user data, creating a privacy or compliance risk if sent to an external vendor. (2) Storing full prompt text as a span attribute creates very high-cardinality, high-volume data that inflates ingestion costs and can ruin dashboard performance. (3) Proprietary prompt templates are intellectual property that should not be exposed to third-party systems.
questions.explanation: Raw prompts combine privacy risk (PII exposure), budget risk (high data volume and cost), and IP risk (proprietary templates) — all of which are controlled by redacting or sampling prompt content before export.
